<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-organized cases, but B stayed closer to the proposition as written by insisting the debate concerns a genuinely privacy-preserving credential (unlinkable, non-identifying), and directly named A's core move—"no government has deployed this"—as a feasibility objection rather than an answer to whether such a mandate, if built to spec, is proportionate. A's strongest material (breach risk, displacement to offshore sites, existing device-level alternatives) was pressed hard and rhetorically vivid ("protection theater," "darker corners"), but its final answer to B's sharpest distinction—that a website-side check still forces effort to overcome even in a negligent household, whereas an unconfigured parental control provides zero boundary—was never squarely rebutted; A just re-asserted that determined minors would route around checks anyway, which doesn't address casual/impulsive users the check would still catch. B's closing crystallized this coverage-gap point cleanly and answered pressure questions with proper A1/A2 structure, giving the more resolved final picture even though A's feasibility pressure was real and not fully neutralized either.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing distinction that a provider-side check "makes access require overcoming it" versus household controls that leave the boundary "absent from the outset" in exactly the negligent-parent scenario A relied on—left largely unanswered in A's final speech.</best_rebuttal>
